1122.dq: a large part of the lexicon of Ghanaian Pidgin is sourced from English and therefore features a cumulative H due to stress-to-tone mapping. (Yakpo 2021); Huber 2013's tone statement is about word/morpheme-level minimal pairs (dè vs dé, wí vs wì).
1122.dloc: Huber 2013 APiCS survey ch. 16, section 4 'Phonology' (tone paragraph); Yakpo 2021 Front. Psychol. 12:690593, AEC tone paragraph and discussion section (Ghanaian Pidgin cumulative H)
1122.prule: No word-stress rule is stated in any reachable source. Huber (2013) describes tone (H vs L) with a 'subordinate' role: it separates grammatical morphemes from homophonous lexical items (dè PROG/HAB vs dé COP, gò FUT vs gó 'go', bì COP vs bí 'bee') and free H-toned pronouns from bound L-toned ones; the survey says nothing about stress placement. Yakpo (2021) classes Ghanaian Pidgin with the African English-lexifier creoles as a two-tone system in which English-sourced words carry one culminative H on the syllable that bears primary stress in the English etymon (stress-to-tone mapping), i.e. H position is lexically inherited, not computed from syllable count or weight.

1122.tone: Huber 2013: 'Tone plays a subordinate role in Ghanaian Pidgin English' -- only grammatical-vs-lexical minimal pairs and pronoun sets; no stress/accent rule given in the survey. Yakpo 2021: Ghanaian Pidgin is a tone language of the African English-lexifier creole type (2T, equipollent /H,L/ or privative /H,0/), English-sourced lexicon has a culminative H placed by stress-to-tone mapping from the English etymon; lexical, grammatical and phrasal tone functions found in his preliminary field data. Neither source describes an independent metrical stress system.

1123.heavy: Counting unit is the mora: every vowel is a mora (long vowels and VV sequences = 2 moras) and nasals can be moraic (coda/syllabic/geminate nasals, e.g. o.o.n 'turtles' = 3 moras; stress on the nasal in (aH ǹ.ti) 'spirit'). No heavy/light syllable dichotomy is invoked; feet may split syllables.
1123.dflt: All-light words (short open syllables only): stress on the penultimate syllable and every third syllable to its left (5th-, 8th-from-last), H pitch on the antepenult; e.g. (kaH.mé.a) 'dog', (aH.rá.na) 'his/her name'.
1123.prule: Stress (intensity/loudness peak) on the penultimate mora of the prosodic word and on every third mora preceding it (right-to-left trimoraic feet whose terminal elements are moras, not syllables); a pitch peak (H) falls on the antepenultimate mora, i.e. the mora before each stress; foot-final mora low in pitch and intensity. Because counting is by mora, long vowels (2 moras) and moraic nasals shift the stressed position relative to syllables, and stress may land on a nasal consonant (aǹ.ti 'spirit').
1123.srule: Rhythmic stresses: a loudness peak on every third mora preceding the penultimate-mora stress (one per right-to-left trimoraic foot, counted in moras), each preceded by a high-pitched mora; the parse of a leftover word-initial one- or two-mora string is 'undetermined by the data'. The source ranks no foot's stress above the others (no primary/secondary distinction reported).

1124.tone: Modern primary reached this compilation: Volk, Erez. 2013. 'Depression as register: Evidence from Mijikenda.' BLS 37: 389-398 (the Internet Archive copy), based on Kisseberth's recordings. Volk analyses Giryama as a privative tone language (/H/ vs zero) with long-distance High Tone Shift: 'This is High Tone Shift in Mijikenda: an underlying high tone (here originating on the third-person singular subject prefix a-) shifts to the right within the phonological phrase, and is heard on the penult.' and 'the final syllable in a phonological phrase in Mijikenda is never pronounced with high pitch.' On prominence he states only: 'Vowel length is not contrastive; the penult is predictably lengthened.' His data (ni-na-ma:la / ni-na-mala ku-gu:la / ni-na-mala ku-gula Ngu:wo) show the lengthening on the phrase-penult only, i.e. non-final words carry no marked length. The words 'stress'/'accent' (prosodic sense) do not occur in Volk 2013. Hyman & Leben 2017 sec. 4.6 (open text) repeat the same Giryama data from Volk 2011:17. So Taylor's 1891 word-penult 'Tonic Accent' corresponds in modern terms to predictable penultimate lengthening (phrase-level in Volk's transcription) plus the penult being the H-docking site; no modern source states or denies a word-stress rule. Volk 2007 MA and Volk 2011 PhD (TAU) remain unreachable.

morph.stmt: Giryama is a canonically prefixing-inflection / suffixing-derivation Bantu language: Ngowa & Ngonyani 2020 p.102, on the verb template SM-NEG-Tense-OM-Root-Extension-Final, 'In both Giryama and Nyanja, mood appears as the final element in the verb structure. All prefixes are inflections, while suffixes include combinations of derivations known as verb extensions and inflections such as mood and aspect'; nouns carry class/number, diminutive and augmentative prefixes with enclitic possessives and a locative ending -ni, and Taylor 1891 (Sketch VII.B) describes deverbal nouns as formed 'usually by means of prefixes, or of alterations in the termination, or by both these together.'

1125.prule: Tone language: every syllable carries its own pitch (High, Mid, Low level tones plus four contour tones on long vowels); verbs have no lexical tone, tone marks tense/mood/negation. Dynamic stress ('Starkton') is secondary and as a rule coincides with a High tone. Only stated quantity-insensitive sub-rule: an affixless noun (Hw) of more than one syllable has a light stress on its FIRST syllable regardless of tone; the noun class prefix is also stressed, and the stem-initial syllable keeps its stress even when lowered after a High prefix. In verb (Zw) forms the (grammatically) High-toned syllable carries the stress; in sentence intonation High tone is always accompanied by stress.

1125.tone: Westermann sec. 23-31: full syllable-tone system (3 level + 4 contour tones), lexical on nouns, grammatical on verbs, plus sentence-tone. 'Starkton' (stress) is described as light, largely parasitic on High tone ('fällt in der Regel mit einem Hochton zusammen'), and regarded by Westermann (sec. 30) as a borrowed, non-original feature. The one tone-independent statement is initial light stress on bare polysyllabic nouns; elsewhere stress placement follows High tone (verb forms, negation, prefixes as demonstratives, sentence focus), i.e. tone- and morphology-conditioned, not a general quantity-insensitive word-stress rule.

evidence_works.detail: Initial main stress is taken from the tradition ('Traditionally it is agreed that Gothic words had initial stress (cf. Krause 1968: 70-72; Jellinek 1926)', p. 153) and then built into a bracketed metrical grid in 'the metrical theory of Halle and Idsardi (1993) and Idsardi (1992) which is adopted here' (p. 152): nonfinal heavy syllables project a right parenthesis, a left parenthesis is placed at the left edge, constituents are built every two elements and are left-headed (rules (6)-(7), p. 154), so that 'The words in (8) are assigned initial stress' (p. 154) and 'initial heavy syllables and initial sequences of two light syllables are organized into single feet, thus producing the prosodic structures required by Prokosch's Law' (p. 154). The foot structure is argued from the Sievers' Law alternation of high vocoids, not from stress observations ('Evidence for the structures that we propose will be provided later', p. 154). Footnote 4 (p. 153): 'In words with some prefixes the main stress does not fall on the absolute initial syllable, but on the initial syllable of the stem', accounted for, following Halle and Vergnaud (1990), by treating those prefixes as non-cyclic morphemes; this matches the entry's compound-verb exception from Wright 1910 sec. 34 (exc_quote). The sentence 'The procedure in (6) and (7) places main stress on the initial syllable in all cases' (p. 157), cited in the row's locator, continues 'as required for Old English' and belongs to the Old English syncope discussion (examples (15)-(17), pp. 156-157), where the Gothic parameter settings 'in (6) and (7) proposed for Gothic' are hypothesized to 'also hold for Old English'; it is not a statement about Gothic and is not relied on here.

tn.quote: In the discussion on tonal patterns in Gua, the syllable would be considered as the tone bearing unit. ... Based on the relative pitch level, tone in Gua exhibits two basic forms. The basic tone levels are low and high. ... Gua is a register tone language which makes use of the height of the pitch to distinguish words. As a register tone language, Gua tones are expected to be realised on relative low and high level pitches. However, it is possible to realise low-high or high-low level pitches (especially on disyllabic words), which are referred to as rising and falling pitches respectively.

1128.dq: Phonological words consist of from one to eight syllables. Their nuclei bear one primary stress. ... The nuclei of the phonological phrases have extra stress and in some cases extra length. Phrases bear intonational contours and obligatory pause at their final borders. (Kondo 1985: 44-45)
1128.heavy: 'long syllable' = syllable with a long vowel or a diphthong: 'The long vowels are of approximately the same length as the diphthongs, and the two (long vowel and diphthong) act in exactly the same way in rules for stress and stress perturbation' (1985: 46); syllable types '(C)V, (C)VV, and CVVV' only, no codas (1985: 44; 2014: 'No tiene sílabas que terminan en consonante'). 2014: 'pesada (contiene vocal larga o diptongo)' vs 'leve... sin vocal larga (subrayada) o una secuencia de vocales (diptongo)'.
1128.dflt: By syllable count in all-light monomorphemes (Kondo 1985 sect. 2.2.1): 2 and 3 syllables -> penult; 4 syllables -> initial in most (8 of 55 antepenult, e.g. bojonavi, tuliquisi, tsapanilu); 5+ 'It has not been determined'. The 2014 dictionary's reader convention is penult unless bracket-marked ([A] 1820, [T] 945, [AT] 51, [U] 25, [P] 3 marks counted in the body by A and B). Kondo 2001 (paraphrase) recasts the 4-syllable split as lexical trochaic (matacabi: initial) vs iambic (tuliquisi: antepenult) footing, so no single default position for longer all-light words. Words whose ONLY long syllable is the word-final one (the long-syllable rule then has no non-final long syllable to select) pattern, tentatively, with the all-light words in 3-syllable words but not in 4-syllable words (Kondo 1985 sect. 2.2.2 p.50): 'It has not yet been fully determined where the stress most commonly occurs on three- and four-syllable words if only the last syllable is long. In fourteen examples of three-syllable words, stress occurs on the penultimate syllable every time, as it does in monomorphemes with no long syllable. However, in ten examples of such four-syllable words, it occurs on the second syllable (antipenultimate) in all, rather than on the initial syllable' (e.g. acávai 'coral snake', apúru 'sardines'; itáboxo 'sky', abálacua 'basket design').
1128.prule: Word stress is weight-sensitive and unbounded: each phonological word (1-8 syllables) bears one primary stress; if the word contains long syllables (long vowel or diphthong; the language has no codas), primary stress falls on the LAST long syllable unless it is word-final, in which case on the second-to-last long syllable (a long final syllable 'always sounds prominent' but is not stressed). In all-light monomorphemes position goes by syllable count: penult in 2- and 3-syllable words, initial in most 4-syllable words (8 of 55 antepenult), 5+ undetermined. Stress is never final in a polysyllabic monomorpheme. Suffixation perturbs stress (short suffixes shift it to the root penult, or to a long root-final syllable). The author hedges the whole: 'neither is there any simple way of predicting stress'; later (2014) 'básicamente predecible, pero las reglas son demasiado complicadas', with Kondo 2001 reanalysing the light-syllable residue as left-to-right binary feet whose trochaic/iambic type is lexically contrastive per morpheme, heavy syllables always stressed, primary on the rightmost non-final foot.
1128.srule: Secondary accents exist; placement not given: 'La palabra tiene un solo acento primario. Si es larga, también puede tener uno o más acentos secundarios (pronunciados con menos fuerza que el acento primario)'; long vowels 'llevan un acento primario o secundario' (Kondo & Kondo 2014: 10, 17; the rules are 'demasiado complicadas' and deferred to Kondo 2001, not opened). Not mentioned in Kondo 1985 (pp.43-55 read: 'Their nuclei bear one primary stress').

1130.dloc: Caudmont 1954 p.200, sec. 1.6 'El acento'; loanword remark p.196
1130.prule: No positional rule: Caudmont states that Guambiano word stress ('acento tónico') can fall on any syllable of the word, that its position is 'fluctuante' and admits no demarcative (edge-based) interpretation, and that its contrastive value in identical context could not be proved; examples carry stress on final (meRapaší, atsimáy), penult (purámpi) and antepenult/earlier (kisímbimera, lamústekən) syllables. He conjectures it is tied to compounding/derivation (stressed root). Branks & Branks 1973 independently list Acento as a suprasegmental phoneme. Coded lexical = free/unpredictable position (not proven contrastive).
1130.srule: Not mentioned in Caudmont 1954 (sec. 1.6 'El acento', p.200; whole article pp.189-206 read): the stress section treats only the position and contrastiveness of the (single) word accent. 1131.prule: Two-tone system (H 'haut plat' vs HL 'descendant') with the syllable as tone-bearing unit; a prosodic unit (lexical word plus affixes/clitics) carries at most one tonal syllable, whose position is lexically specified (every tone-by-position schema attested in 2- and 3-syllable units, e.g. trisyllables H.∅.∅, ∅.H.∅, ∅.∅.H, HL.∅.∅, ∅.HL.∅, ∅.∅.HL; in 4-syllable units HL on any syllable but H only on the 4th, in finite verbs; in 5-syllable units only HL on the 1st or 3rd syllable, H on the 5th, or no tone are attested); atonal syllables receive L and surface tones follow from two sandhi rules (HL simplification, H reassociation). No stress rule is stated for Wobzi.

1131.tone: Lai analyses Wobzi Khroskyabs word prosody as a culminative two-tone system (H vs HL, minimal pair jlé ‘lapin’ vs jlê ‘flûte’), at most one tone per prosodic unit, position unpredictable/lexical; no word-stress rule is given. For the Phosul dialect Lai reports Sun (2008b): 'dans les exemples polysyllabiques, seule une syllabe peut porter un ton (et cette syllabe est la seule syllabe accentuée), et nous ne pouvons pas prédire quelle est la syllabe porteuse de ton' — i.e. the tonal syllable is equated with the accented one, its location lexical. Functionally pitch-accent-like (culminative, lexical placement) but described by the author as tone + sandhi, not stress.

tn.translation: The unit liable to bear a tone in Wobzi Khroskyabs is the syllable. We distinguish two tones. A high level tone and a falling tone. ... we use H for the high level tone and HL for the falling tone. The phonological representations of the minimal pair jlé 'rabbit' vs. jlê 'flute' ... Besides the two types of tonal syllables, Wobzi also has toneless syllables ... We define the prosodic unit in Wobzi Khroskyabs as a sequence of syllables sharing at most a single tone, which governs all the tone sandhi within that sequence.

1140.prule: Primary stress targets the penultimate syllable but must be foot-initial, and feet are built on morpheme boundaries (each pre-root morpheme a foot; root+TAM suffix one foot): stress falls on the rightmost non-final foot-initial (normally morpheme-initial, typically root-initial) syllable, shifting leftward to the 3rd/4th/5th-last when the penult is not morpheme-initial; monosyllables stressed on their only syllable. 1140.srule: Every foot, even a monosyllabic one, carries secondary stress on its first syllable; since feet are the morpheme-aligned units of the primary rule (each pre-root prefix; root+TAM), secondary stresses fall on the initial syllables of all non-primary feet and are predictable from the foot boundaries (not transcribed). 1141.prule: One invariable main stress per word whose position 'is not predictable except within certain inflectional patterns' (sec. 5a); stress position alone distinguishes otherwise identical forms (xu'a 'laughter' vs x'ua 'laugh!', xas'a 'goodness' vs x'asa 'good (f.sg.)', m'ara 'it is a snake' vs mar'a 'they bring'). In the noun lexicon, stems end either in a stressed vowel (-'a, -'i, -'o, -'u, -'e) or in unstressed -a, -i (sec. 6b: tut'a 'dog' vs d'ala 'bitch', yakan'a 'wild boar' vs mang'awa 'cow'; kit'a 'cat' 'has irregular stress'); polysyllabic verbal past stems are lexically initial- or final-stressed (sec. 23: 'asari-, w'iard- vs aw'ird-, far'a-). Within inflection, stress is fixed by a precedence hierarchy of morphemes (sec. 30: negative prefixes > preverb suffixes -an'a/-ar'a/-aw'a > modal prefix b(i)- or initial stress of Pres. Subjunctive/Imperative/Past Conditional > personal endings / past stem / past participle); several nominal suffixes (definite -'a, obl. pl. -'a) are inherently stressed, and the vocative without a particle brings stress forward to the first syllable.
1141.srule: Words or phrases of three or more syllables may carry a secondary stress [ˌ]. Its position is not at a fixed distance from the main stress (pretonic 1-3 syllables or posttonic 1-5 syllables in MacKenzie's examples, e.g. nˌištānerˈa 'I sat down', nˈaništabenerˌa 'I had not sat down') but is set, like the main stress, by the fixed precedence of inherently stressed morphemes: in verbal forms the stress of the out-ranked stress-bearing element (preverb suffix under a negative prefix; modal prefix / initial subjunctive stress under a preverb; personal ending under a modal or negative prefix, e.g. mˈakarˌu 'I do not do', bˈıdaymˌe 'that we give') surfaces as a secondary word stress, and is often lost entirely when out-ranked by two classes.

However, nothing in the Haisla data would argue against taking the Kwakwala rule as basic.' Werle 2010 sec. 4.2 (local cache, verified): 'Prominence is contrastive only in Haisla and Heiltsukvla. Haisla stress is intensity or low tone (V̀) (Vink 1977, Lincoln and Rath 1980, Bach 1989)', citing pairs ɢʷàlas 'lizard' vs ɢʷalàs 'quitting time', ʔìxʔika 'swing hammer' vs ʔixʔikà 'eat balanced diet'. 1148.dq: 1.3.4 Predictability of syllable division, stress, and position of vowel length within a phonological word.
1148.dloc: section 1.3.4 'Predictability of syllable division, stress, and position of vowel length within a phonological word', pp. 12-15 (archive.org leaves n23-n26); suprasegmental inventory 1.1.4 on p. 2 (leaf n13)
1148.heavy: In disyllables a closed (CVC) second syllable attracts stress, unless the first syllable contains the low vowel /a/ (then initial stress). Vowel length is derived from stress, not a conditioner. In 3+-syllable words a final VCVV sequence shifts stress from penult to antepenult.
1148.dflt: penultimate (= initial in disyllables; penult in words of three or more syllables)
1148.prule: Word stress is non-phonemic and predictable. Monosyllables: heavy stress. Disyllables: stress the second syllable if it is closed AND the first syllable's vowel is not /a/; otherwise stress the first syllable. Words of 3+ syllables: heavy stress on the penult, except words ending in a VCVV sequence, which take antepenultimate stress. Remaining syllables weakly stressed.
1148.srule: Not mentioned in Kaushikkar 1972, section 1.3.4 (pp. 12-15 read): the source describes only two degrees, one heavy (tonic) stress per word and weak (unmarked) stress on all remaining syllables ('The remaining syllables are weakly stressed.', p. 14); no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.
